items.title: Jones Hank — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] It’s interesting, the point you make about Tatum. I think a similar thing is said about Coltrane.

ctx.x: Yes, I think that's it. I think a lot of it is visual as well. If it looks like it is happening, then they perceive it as happening. That is them that is as far as they know. They are not into it as much. Maybe, they haven't thought about it at the correct level. They go to be entertained, not to listen. Entertainment is one thing, and listening and enjoyment is something else. They are two type of things.

It’s interesting, the point you make about Tatum. I think a similar thing is said about Coltrane. A lot of people try to emulate where he took the saxophone solo. But, there is only one Coltrane, there's only one Art Tatum. There is only one Sarah Vaughan.

That is very true. You see, some people… If you can make it a liable presentation, or a viable concept, then it is relevant. But, I keep thinking about what Earl Hines did. You have to learn what to leave out. What he meant was, you have to leave that anything that does not contribute to the whole in a meaningful manner. If it does not contribute to the body of the work that you are trying to do, if it has no meaning, what is it doing there?
